### 2026-10-09 04:58:09 UTC · **Claude**

The hackathon is **tomorrow, Friday Oct 9** in San Francisco. You need to be approved on Luma to get in, so check your registration status today.

I read the main page, the project gallery, the Luma event page and the sponsor links. The submit form needs a sign-in, so I couldn't see its fields. The gallery is empty for now.

## The basics
- **Name:** Cyberdefense Hackathon, hosted by tokens& during SF Tech Week
- **Venue:** AWS Builder Loft, SF. Luma only shows the exact address after you register.
- **Theme:** Build defensive AI that finds threats, understands attacks, or helps fix vulnerabilities. You need a working project by the end of the day. The four focus areas:
  1. **Threat discovery:** find vulnerabilities, misconfigurations and attack paths before attackers do
  2. **Attack intelligence:** turn scattered signals into a clear picture of what's happening
  3. **Autonomous remediation:** patch, harden and verify fixes with little human help
  4. **Continuous defense:** systems that keep monitoring, adapting and responding
- **Teams:** up to 4 people, one project per team. Solo builders are also welcome.
- **Rule:** the project must be built during the event.

## Schedule (PT)
| Time | What |
|---|---|
| 9:30 AM | Doors open + opening remarks |
| 11:00 AM | Kickoff & hacking starts (submissions open 11:30) |
| 1:30 PM | Lunch |
| **4:30 PM** | **Submission deadline** |
| 5:00 PM | Finalist demos + judging |
| 7:00 PM | Awards + closing |

That's about 5.5 hours of hacking.

## What you need to do before the event
1. **Get approved on Luma** at [luma.com/cyberhack](https://luma.com/cyberhack). Approval is required, and pending or unapproved people won't be let in at the door.
2. **Register separately with AWS Builder Loft.** This is in addition to the Luma RSVP, and the link is on the Luma page.
3. **Bring a physical government photo ID.** Digital IDs aren't accepted, and you must be 18+.
4. There's no parking on site, and bikes and scooters aren't allowed inside.
5. Join the Discord: https://bit.ly/discord-17
6. Make an account on tokens& ahead of time (Google or an email code). You need it to submit at https://tokensand.com/cyberhack/submit.

## What to submit (by 4:30 PM)
- A GitHub repo the reviewers can access
- A short demo video with a shareable link
- A description of what you built and the tools you used
- Your team members' names and contact emails
- Optional: a working website and a screenshot of the project

## Sponsor prizes
| Sponsor | Track | Prizes |
|---|---|---|
| **ClickHouse** (real-time analytics database) | Best use of real-time analytics | 1st: $1,000 gift card + $500 credits · 2nd: $500 + $300 credits · 3rd: $250 |
| **Semgrep** (code security) | Best vulnerability found by Semgrep | 1st: $1,000 · 2nd: $500 · both get 20 Semgrep credits |
| **Guild.ai** (platform for running AI agents) | Best use of Guild to host and run agents | Winner: $1,000 · two runners-up: $500 each |
| **Akash** (GPU compute marketplace, AkashML for inference) | Best use case of Akash | $500 / $250 / $150 in Akash credits |
| **Pi** (agentic product security) | Most Innovative | 1st–3rd: Elgato Stream Deck + gift card. Pi is only a prize sponsor; you won't get access to its product at this event. |

More detail on how some tracks are judged:
- **ClickHouse:** judged on data scale, query/response latency, and how directly the insights drive detection, fixes or monitoring.
- **Semgrep:** for the most unique or interesting vulnerability found in AI-generated code. Setup in Claude Code is to run `claude plugin install semgrep@claude-plugins-official`, restart, then sign in through the browser popup. It's a free public beta with no card needed. If access is blocked, ask the Semgrep team at the event.

Docs: [ClickHouse](https://clickhouse.com/docs) · [Akash](https://akash.network/docs/) · [Guild.ai](https://docs.guild.ai/) · [Semgrep quickstart](https://docs.semgrep.dev/semgrep-guardian/quickstart)

Other partners listed: OpenAI, MongoDB and ElevenLabs. They're named, but no prizes are listed for them.

## People
- **Speakers:** people from Guild.ai, Akash (founder), Pi (CEO), ClickHouse and Semgrep.
- **Judges (11):** people from Pi, OpenAI, Guild.ai, AWS, Akash, ClickHouse, Semgrep, Airbyte, FlowiseAI/Workday and Visibl Semiconductors.

## How to approach it
One project can compete in several sponsor tracks at once. For example, an agent hosted on Guild could run Semgrep over AI-generated code, send the findings into ClickHouse for real-time detection dashboards, and run inference on Akash. That would cover four sponsor tracks plus Most Innovative. Have the repo and a recorded demo ready well before 4:30. The video is required, and it's the piece people usually leave too late.

I can set up a starter repo tonight with the Semgrep plugin installed and a ClickHouse schema scaffolded, or brainstorm project ideas aimed at those tracks.

### 2026-10-09 05:07:01 UTC · **Claude**

Here are four ideas. Each one covers at least four of the five prize tracks. All of them use the same building blocks:

- **Semgrep** scans the code.
- **ClickHouse** stores and queries the events or findings.
- **AkashML** runs open models for triage and patches.
- **Guild** hosts the agent. From its docs, Guild agents can be started by webhooks or schedules and come with GitHub and Slack integrations.

None of the four depends on Pi's product, which isn't available at the event, so Pi's "Most Innovative" prize is open to all of them.

| # | Idea | Tracks | Time risk | Demo impact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Attack-to-Patch | All 5 | High | Highest |
| 2 | Which LLM writes the least secure code (benchmark) | All 5 | Low | High |
| 3 | Monitor for coding agents | 4 (Semgrep is weak here) | Medium | High |
| 4 | Guard on AI-written PRs | All 5 | Low | Medium |

---

### 1. Attack-to-Patch: from a live attack to a merged fix
A deliberately vulnerable web app gets hit by a replayed attack (SQL injection, path traversal, SSRF). The pipeline follows the attack all the way to a fix.
- **ClickHouse:** takes in a large stream of request logs (millions of rows, mostly normal traffic) and flags the attack with detection queries that update as data arrives.
- **Guild:** an alert starts an agent through a webhook. The agent maps the targeted endpoint to the route handler in the repo.
- **Semgrep:** confirms the vulnerable line.
- **Akash:** an open model writes the patch.
- **Guild:** opens a PR, then replays the attack to confirm it's blocked.
- **Demo:** a timer from the first malicious request to the merged fix, aiming for under 90 seconds.
- **Why it's strong:** it covers detection, understanding and remediation in one loop, which matches the event's theme directly. ClickHouse's judging criteria (data scale, latency, insight that drives a fix) fit it closely.
- **Risk:** many moving parts. Fake the hard parts: generate the logs synthetically and keep the vulnerable app tiny, with about 5 endpoints.

### 2. Which LLM writes the least secure code? A live benchmark
- **Akash:** have 4–6 open models on AkashML each generate code for 200+ security-relevant prompts (file upload, auth, SQL, deserialization, shell commands).
- **Semgrep:** scan every output.
- **ClickHouse:** store every finding, tagged by model, prompt, CWE category and language. Show a live leaderboard and a heatmap of vulnerabilities by model and category.
- **Guild:** an agent runs the benchmark on a schedule and posts the changes to Slack.
- **Why it's strong:** the Semgrep prize is for the "most unique or interesting" vulnerability found in AI-generated code. Generating thousands of samples is how you find a strange one. It also uses Akash heavily for inference and gives ClickHouse real data volume. It's close to model-eval work, so it plays to your background.
- **Risk:** low. It's mostly batch jobs and a dashboard. The main risk is rate limits on AkashML, so start generating early.

### 3. Monitor for coding agents
The event's Luma page highlights AI systems escaping controlled environments, and this idea targets that directly.
- **Capture:** Claude Code hooks (or any agent's tool-call log) record every action the agent takes: shell commands, file reads, network calls.
- **ClickHouse:** detection queries that update in real time look for bad behaviour: reading `.env` and then `curl` to an unknown host, `chmod` on files outside the workspace, sudden bursts of tool calls.
- **Akash:** a model classifies whether the activity looks malicious.
- **Guild:** an agent responds by pausing the session, sending a Slack alert or reverting the change.
- **Semgrep:** scans files the agent wrote before they're saved. This is the weakest link to a track, but it works.
- **Why it's strong:** it's the most novel of the four and the best candidate for Most Innovative. You could demo it with a red-team prompt that tries to steal a secret, and show the monitor catching it live.
- **Risk:** medium. Hooking into the agent is easy; the work is in making the detection rules convincing.

### 4. Guard on AI-written PRs
- **Guild:** a GitHub webhook starts an agent on every PR.
- **Semgrep:** scans the diff.
- **Akash:** a model explains each finding and suggests a fix as a review comment.
- **ClickHouse:** tracks findings by author type (human vs. each AI tool) over time.
- **Why it's strong:** easiest to finish and clearly useful.
- **Risk:** low, but the demo feels like a product many teams already sell. This is your fallback if things go badly.

---

## My recommendation
**Build #2 as the core and add #1's patch loop if time allows.**

- #2 can be finished in 5.5 hours even if something breaks, and it gives you the best chance at the Semgrep prize.
- Once the benchmark data is flowing, add a step where the Guild agent takes the worst finding, has Akash patch it and Semgrep re-scan it. Now you have a remediation story too.
- If you have a team of 3–4, do #1 instead: it has the highest upside and the work splits cleanly by component.

**Rough plan for #2 (11:00 → 4:30):**
| Time | Task |
|---|---|
| 11:00–11:45 | Get AkashML, Semgrep, ClickHouse and Guild accounts working. Write the prompt set (do this tonight). |
| 11:45–1:30 | Generation runs on Akash → Semgrep → ClickHouse ingest. Start long runs before lunch. |
| 1:30–3:00 | ClickHouse queries + leaderboard and heatmap dashboard. Guild scheduled agent. |
| 3:00–3:45 | Optional patch loop (patch the worst finding, re-scan). |
| 3:45–4:15 | Record the demo video, write the README, pick your Semgrep finding to submit. |
| 4:15–4:30 | Submit. |

### 2026-10-09 05:57:03 UTC · **Claude**

Build one system where all five sponsors are on the critical path, not five separate add-ons. The idea that ties it together: ClickHouse analytics decide which vulnerability gets a fixer agent, and the system checks that the fixer didn't just fool the scanner. The full report is at [reports/Cyberdefense hackathon winning strategy.md](Cyberdefense%20hackathon%20winning%20strategy.md).

**The design: a governed "security eval arena"**
1. **Generate:** several open models on AkashML write code for security-relevant tasks. Using multiple open models is the Akash story.
2. **Scan:** Semgrep scans every output. The live demo uses the Guardian plugin; custom rules supply the unusual finding.
3. **Score:** findings stream into ClickHouse. A spawn score, computed in SQL, decides whether a fixer agent is worth launching. It combines how many models produced the same bug, how often each rule was right in this run, whether the bug is reachable, severity, past fix success rates and cost.
4. **Fix and check:** a fixer patches the code. A verifier re-tests it with an exploit and a second set of rules. An adversarial auditor checks the patch for cheats like a `nosemgrep` comment or moved code.
5. **Learn:** a rule-writer agent turns repeated verified fixes into a new Semgrep rule and re-runs it against every model.
6. **Govern:** Guild hosts the agents. The demo shows the agent tree, a human approval step before any merge, and a live block when an injected prompt tries to delete the repo.

**Why this fits the judges**
- **Pi:** their thesis is that finding bugs is solved and the gap is remembering, fixing, finding variants and preventing recurrence. The fix → generalize → new rule loop says exactly that.
- **Pi's CEO (a speaker, not a judge):** he ran vulnerability response at Microsoft, so he will expect proof the bug is exploitable.
- **Semgrep:** their product team is focused on reducing noisy findings in AI-written code. They want one true, novel finding, not a dump.
- **ClickHouse:** the judge writes about agents querying ClickHouse through its MCP connector. Show insight that triggers an action, with timings from the query log.
- **Guild:** their pitch is governance — scoped credentials, approval steps and audit trails — not just hosting.
- **Akash:** the founder's theme is sovereign, decentralized compute.
- **Independent judges:**
  - The Airbyte and Visibl judges both describe "self-test, then a human approves" loops.
  - Flowise's founder will want a clearly drawn agent graph with a human approval step.
- Identity confidence: medium for the AWS judge and the two Pi engineers.

**The five risks that matter**
1. **AkashML inside Guild:** Guild can't point at a custom model endpoint, and its runtime blocks outbound internet. AkashML has to be wrapped as a Guild custom integration. Try this tonight; if it fails, the Guild and Akash stories both fail.
2. **Semgrep's fixed ruleset:** the Guardian plugin can't load custom rules. A unique finding needs a custom taint rule run through the CLI.
   - Best targets are agent-specific bugs: model output flowing into `eval` or a shell, or MCP tool inputs flowing into a shell or network call.
   - Generate the vulnerable code honestly on stage; don't plant it by hand.
3. **Guild's task cap:** by default an agent run is capped at 50 agent tasks. Fan out within one agent rather than spawning many.
4. **AkashML limits:** rate limits and exact model IDs aren't published. Call `/v1/models` first.
5. **Finalist screen:** only finalists demo at 5:00, so the README and video are likely what gets you picked between 4:30 and 5:00. Record the video before 4:30 no matter what.

### 2026-10-09 06:10:29 UTC · **Claude**

# Final idea: **PROOF**, a security arena where agents have to prove their fixes

**One-liner:** Open models write code, Semgrep finds what they got wrong, and ClickHouse decides which bugs are worth fixing based on evidence. Fixer agents must pass independent checks before a person approves the merge. Every verified fix becomes a new guardrail that protects future PRs.

## How ideas 1, 2 and 4 fit together

| Earlier idea | Its role in PROOF | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| **#2 LLM security benchmark** | **The Arena** produces the code and the model leaderboard | Scale and cross-model data: "4 of 5 models make this same mistake" |
| **#1 Attack-to-Patch** | **Runtime evidence**: the arena's worst generated app runs as a sandboxed target on Akash, and its traffic logs stream into ClickHouse | Proof a bug actually matters ("this vulnerable route is being probed right now"), plus a fix check against real traffic |
| **#4 AI-PR guard** | **The front door**: a Guild GitHub trigger scans every AI-written PR | Real-world use: the rules minted from the arena protect actual repos |

Each idea alone has been done before. Together they form one loop: **generate → detect → prioritize with evidence → fix → prove → mint a guardrail → enforce it on PRs → update the leaderboard.** I didn't find any project or benchmark in the research that closes this whole loop.

## The three signature features (the innovation pitch)

### 1. Evidence-based spawn decisions: analytics decide who fixes what
A fixer agent is spawned only when ClickHouse evidence justifies the cost. The score combines three independent signals:
- **Static:** Semgrep's dataflow trace and severity, weighted by how often that rule was right *in this run*.
- **Consensus:** how many different models made the same mistake on the same task. A mistake many models share is a systemic risk, not a one-off bug.
- **Runtime:** whether the vulnerable route appears in live traffic on the Akash-hosted target.

The score also uses the success rate of past fixes for this bug type (from memory) and the expected cost and time per fix. Every spawn decision shows its own breakdown, so judges can see *why* agent B was sent to fix agent A's finding.

### 2. Proof of fix: "Semgrep-clean" alone doesn't count as fixed
2026 research found that "the scanner stopped flagging it" overstates fix success. One study measured 1.83×; that figure came from secondary sources, so check it before quoting it on stage. Every patch has to pass four gates:
1. The existing tests still pass, so functionality is preserved.
2. An **independent** ruleset re-scans the patch (not the one that found the bug).
3. The suspicious request from the logs is replayed against the patched build in the sandbox and is now rejected.
4. An **anti-cheat auditor** looks for suppression comments, code that was moved rather than fixed, or new weaknesses the patch introduced.

Headline metric: **the inflation ratio**, meaning fixes that looked done divided by fixes that passed all four gates, broken down by model.

### 3. Guardrail minting: find one bug, prevent the whole class
When a fix passes all four gates, a rule-writer agent turns it into a **new custom Semgrep rule**. The rule is then:
- re-run against every model's output in the arena: "this rule finds the bug in output from 4 of 5 models"
- added to the PR guard, so future AI-written PRs are blocked from repeating it
- credited on the leaderboard against the model that would have introduced the bug

This loop also produces the Semgrep prize entry.

## Agent roster (all hosted on Guild)

| Agent | Job | Platform / access |
|---|---|---|
| **Orchestrator** | Runs the whole session and fans out to the other agents | Guild agent; holds the human approval step |
| **Generator** | Writes code for agent-style tasks, fanned out across 4–5 models | AkashML (wrapped as a Guild custom integration) |
| **Scanner** | Runs Semgrep: the Guardian plugin for the live demo, the command line with custom rules for depth | Read-only access to the repo |
| **Analyst / dispatcher** | Reads spawn scores and decides which fixes to launch | ClickHouse MCP server, read-only |
| **Fixer** | Patches the bug: tries a cheap AkashML model first, escalates to a stronger one if a gate fails | Cannot open PRs itself |
| **Verifier** | Runs the four proof gates | Sandbox only |
| **Anti-cheat auditor** | Checks the patch diff for gaming the scanner and newly introduced bugs | Read-only |
| **Rule-writer** | Mints and validates new Semgrep rules | Can write only to the rules folder |
| **PR guard** | Triggered by GitHub PR events; enforces the minted rules | Comments on PRs only |

**Governance demo:** a code comment in the scanned code carries a hidden instruction to take a destructive action. Guild's credential policy denies it live, and the denial appears in the audit log. A human approves every merge.

## Memory strategy

- **Episodic (past fixes):** ClickHouse `fix_attempts` table, one row per attempt with the model, bug type, which gates passed, cost and time. It feeds the fix-success rate in the spawn score.
- **Semantic (bug patterns):** ClickHouse materialized views of bug rates by model and by bug type, plus a short "known patterns" note in Guild's shared workspace context that every agent reads.
- **Procedural (playbooks):** the minted Semgrep rules, version-controlled in the repo.
- **Write policy:**
  - Only fixes that passed all four gates are saved to memory, each with a record of the run, model and evidence that produced it.
  - Revoking a fix cascades to every rule derived from it.
  - Content read from scanned code or tool output is treated as untrusted and can't be saved to memory directly. This defends against memory poisoning.

## Analytics: the core tables and queries

- `generations` (model, task, code hash, tokens, latency)
- `findings` (rule, bug type, severity, dataflow, model, route, root-cause cluster)
- `traffic` (route, status, flags, timestamp)

### 2026-10-09 07:05:24 UTC · **Claude**

Use Tripwire as the base and add PROOF's fix-and-prevent loop on top. If you had to pick one of the two exactly as written, Tripwire is the better choice. The merged version can win more prizes for about 90 extra minutes after lunch.

The full review and plan are in [Tripwire vs PROOF — Review and Merged Plan](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/759fb797-b121-4065-be4a-23f8d0457273).

**Why Tripwire is the stronger base**
- **Demo:** an agent being caught and blocked within seconds is easier for judges to follow than PROOF's nine-agent loop.
- **ClickHouse:** 30M rows, `windowFunnel` rules and an alert that blocks the agent make it the stronger ClickHouse entry.
- **Risk:** it uses fake tools and generated data, and must work end to end by 1:30, so it's the safer build.
- **Measurement:** it reports catch rate on 30 attacks and 30 tricky normal cases, detect and contain times, and cost per 1,000 events.

**Where it falls short**
- **No Semgrep:** the brief doesn't use Semgrep at all, which leaves $1,000 / $500 on the table.
- **Guild is an afterthought:** containment only happens "if its API allows". The brief also says Guild's prize is unconfirmed, but the hackathon page lists it: $1,000 plus two $500 runners-up.
- **Stops at containment:** Pi's view is that finding problems is the easy part and fixing and preventing them is the gap. Tripwire never gets to the fix.
- **OpenAI and ElevenLabs:** neither has a prize, and the voice briefing costs build time for nothing.
- **Smaller technical gaps:**
  - Detection is signature-only.
  - The same people write the rules and the test cases.
  - The checkpoint needs a stable public URL for Guild to reach it.

**What to keep from PROOF**
- Replaying the attack as proof that the fix works.
- A custom Semgrep rule run on the agents' own AI-written code.
- A new Semgrep rule and Guild policy as the "never again" ending.
- Guild's approval step and policy changes.

Drop PROOF's multi-model code arena and its cross-model spawn score; there isn't time for both projects.

**The merged loop, step by step**
1. Agents hosted on Guild send every tool call through the checkpoint, which runs on Akash Console.
2. ClickHouse stores the events and runs the detection rules.
3. A small open model on AkashML double-checks anything flagged.
4. Guild blocks the agent.
5. An investigator traces the attack to a line in the agent's AI-written code, and a Semgrep rule pinpoints it.
6. A fixer patches it, and the same attack is replayed and refused.
7. A human approves the restore, and the new rule and policy apply to every agent.

**Today's plan:** keep your friend's timeline, roles and 1:30 deadline exactly. The cure loop only starts if the core works by 1:30, and it replaces the voice briefing in the 2:00–3:15 window. If you fall behind, cut the cure loop.

**One honesty rule:** the agents' code must be written live at kickoff. If it turns out to have no flaw, report that rather than planting one.

The doc is private until you share it from its Share menu.

### 2026-10-09 07:30:58 UTC · **Claude**

I combined both plans into one build plan for the day: [Tripwire — Final Build Plan](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/bb32ce25-ec2a-4b0d-8bf0-fc3268ad51cd).

Tripwire is the core and has to catch and block an attack end to end by 1:30. PROOF's cure loop (find the root cause, fix it, replay the attack to prove the fix, add a guardrail) is built after lunch and is the first thing cut if you fall behind.

The plan includes:
- each prize track's published requirement, how you meet it, what judges will see, and who owns it
- every component and where it runs
- starting ClickHouse tables, detection queries and a Semgrep rule
- how you'll measure results
- an hour-by-hour schedule with owners and a "done when" check
- risks and fallbacks
- the demo script and judge questions
- the before-kickoff and submission checklists

The SQL and the Semgrep rule are starting points I haven't run, so test them early.

**Date check:** the hackathon is Friday, October 9, and my clock says that's today, not tomorrow. If so, the before-kickoff checklist is due this morning.

**Ask at kickoff:** whether Guild can change an agent's permissions while it's running. The plan works either way, because the checkpoint's own blocklist is the fallback.

The doc is private until you share it from its Share menu, so your friend can't open it until you do.

### 2026-10-09 17:53:48 UTC · **Claude**

Here's what to set up on each, in priority order.

### 1. ClickHouse Cloud (your screenshot): create it, with these tweaks
- **Database:** ClickHouse ✓ · **Provider:** AWS ✓
- **Name:** `tripwire`
- **Region:** change Ohio to **Oregon (us-west-2)** if it's in the list. We're in SF, and every hold-mode decision does a ClickHouse lookup on the hot path, so a nearby region gives visibly better latency numbers. Keep Ohio if Oregon isn't offered.
- **Replicas:** leave the default (2).
- **Max size per replica:** drop it to the smallest option. 30M rows is small, and a lower ceiling protects your trial credits. Min 16 GiB is fine.
- **Advanced:** leave TDE off. Crash reports are your choice.

**After you click Create:**
1. **Save the password right away.** It's shown only once.
2. **IP access list:** choose "add my current IP". Sripadha on the same venue Wi-Fi shares that public IP. Only use "anywhere" if one of you is on a different network.
3. **Settings → idling:** set it to never idle, or the longest option. Otherwise the first query after a quiet spell stalls for a while, and that could happen mid-demo.
4. Put the values in `.env` (not in chat, not in git). `.env` is gitignored:
   ```
   CLICKHOUSE_HOST=<xxxx>[clickhouse-cloud-host]
   CLICKHOUSE_PORT=8443
   CLICKHOUSE_SECURE=1
   CLICKHOUSE_USER=default
   CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=<the one-time password>
   ```
   Then I run `make db && make seed && make load ROWS=30000000`. The 30M rows are generated on the server, so nothing is uploaded over the Wi-Fi.

The main reason to use Cloud: your checkpoint and Sripadha's detector then read and write one shared database from two laptops. With 2 replicas, freshly inserted rows can briefly be invisible to a read, so once you switch I'll add a read-after-write consistency setting to the shared client.

### 2. AkashML (`playground.akashml.com`): needed now, for Sripadha
- Create **one API key** named `tripwire`. It goes in `AKASHML_API_KEY`.
- Note your **free credit balance** and the **model list**, then give Sripadha two models:
  - `AKASHML_MODEL_SMALL`: the fastest one. Hold mode has a 3-second budget.
  - `AKASHML_MODEL_LARGE`: the strongest one, from a **different family**, for the investigator and the two-model quorum.
- The key goes in the `.env` of whichever laptop runs the AI code. On demo day, when everything runs on one machine, it must be in that machine's `.env`.

### 3. Guild (`settings/api-keys`): hold off on most of it
- **Now:** run `guild auth login` in a terminal (browser sign-in; no key needed for the CLI).
- **Around 2:30, when Sripadha publishes the Guild agent:** create an **API trigger** on that agent. Its key is shown once and goes in `GUILD_TRIGGER_KEY`, with the trigger URL in `GUILD_TRIGGER_URL`. My `/guild/run` button uses these.

The Akash Console key is valid. `/v1/user/me` returned 200 with your account, and `/v1/deployments` shows **0 deployments**, so nothing has been created and nothing is costing money. It's stored in the gitignored `.env`.

**Where it could fit.** Sripadha's Guild-hosted agent has to reach our checkpoint over a **public HTTPS URL**, because Guild agents can't call a laptop on venue Wi-Fi. There are two ways to provide that:

1. **A tunnel from my laptop** (`cloudflared` or `ngrok`). Fastest and free. The catch is that a free tunnel gets a new URL on every restart, and Guild locks the URL once the integration is published, so the tunnel has to stay up through the demo.
2. **Run the checkpoint on Akash Console**, pointed at ClickHouse Cloud. This gives a stable public URL and puts Akash compute on the critical path next to AkashML, which strengthens the Akash prize story. It costs a little money and adds deployment risk (whether HTTPS works on the provider's ingress, latency, keeping the live stream stable). It also depends on the Cloud IP allowlist being fixed: an Akash host has its own IP, which would need adding too, or Cloud set to allow "anywhere" for today.

My recommendation: decide at the **3:00 Guild go/no-go**. Use option 1 by default. Try option 2 only if the core and signature demos are already green by then, and only with your explicit go-ahead before I deploy anything.

### 2026-10-09 20:16:02 UTC · **Claude**

I fixed the Semgrep finding, and Guild now works end to end, including the human-approval step. Everything below is merged to `main`; the latest commit is `1c47f0e`.

**The Semgrep fix**
- **Prompt injection (the real finding):** our hold check no longer puts the agent-chosen destination host into the free-text line it sends to AkashML; the host now reaches the model only inside the fenced event data. A test confirms it, and a live re-check shows the attack is still judged malicious (confidence 0.9–1.0, about 1.3–1.5 s) with no false positives on normal operations.
- **Path-like agent ids:** the checkpoint now rejects agent ids that could be rewritten into another endpoint (the lead from the scan).
- **Still open:** the scan keeps reporting the finding until Sripadha fences the prompt builder in `ai/quick_check.py` and the detector's context. I've asked him in the status file.

**Guild, live:**
- Guild's integration test reached our checkpoint through the tunnel and proxy (HTTP 200).
- I attached a real Tripwire integration to your `tripwire-deploy-bot` and republished it. Run from Tripwire, it made three tool calls through the checkpoint, and all were allowed.
- When we prompted it to also post to an outside host, hold mode **denied** the send. The agent reported that denial itself in its Guild session.
- The cure panel has a new **Ask a human in Guild** button. It sends the real incident and proof to your `tripwire-responder`, which drafts the case and waits for a person to reply APPROVE or REJECT in Guild. Tripwire does not read that reply automatically; you still click Approve in Tripwire.

**Also done:**
- **Console:** ⌘K command palette; a confusion matrix that fills only from real eval counts; a detection-latency histogram and a sparkline built from real timings.
- **README:** statuses updated to what's verified, plus 4 live screenshots.
- **Video:** `docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md` has the shot list, narration, a pre-take checklist and a Wi-Fi fallback.
- **Provenance:** the exporter is ready; it refuses to write the file if any secret remains. It runs at 3:15.
- **Sripadha's eval scenarios:** I merged his 60 cases (30 attack, 30 benign); all 60 validate.

Tests: 205 unit and integration tests pass, plus the 16 end-to-end checks.

**The demo stack is running on your laptop now:** checkpoint, detector, Guild proxy and tunnel. The console is at http://localhost:8000. Don't run `make dev`, because it would clash with the stack on port 8000. **Don't stop the tunnel:** your Guild integration's URL is tied to it, and a restart means rebuilding the integration.

**Next:** I'm self-pacing and will check again at **1:46 PT**. If Sripadha's outbreak tracing (Act 3) or eval runner (Act 5) hasn't landed by then, I'll build what's missing, as agreed.
